synopsis: EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 is the booklet’s only identified standard formally allowing validated simulation to extend acceptance to new conditions and modified vehicles; informative Annex T addresses simulated on-track tests, while Annex U addresses acceptance extension for vehicles of the same basic design [f14672, f15362]. Physical running tests remain the reference anchor: they validate the model before simulation extends conditions, assesses vehicle modifications or compares against an approved reference vehicle [f8136, f14675]. DynoTRAIN developed the validation method, with results published in 2014–2015, drawing on multiple models, tools, vehicles and countries and more than 1,000 simulations; unscalable engineering-judgment review motivated objective metrics [f14677, f7711, f7712]. Agreement is assessed using at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons per quantity from at least 12 track sections, with limits on means and standard deviations across the comparison set [f14680]. The booklet rates rail as its strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking, advocating similarity arguments, documented changes and targeted bridging tests, but transfers the acceptance mechanism rather than the much more deterministic wheel-rail physics [f8137, f15373, f14682]. No percentage of physical tests actually removed across rail certifications was published, and no documented accident in which an EN 14363-validated simulation itself created false confidence was found [f7856, f7990].
